item.title: In Silicon Valley, AI companies are poaching talent from tech giants
item.description: Corporations like OpenAI and Anthropic are looking to build teams in countries like India and Singapore.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published in Rest of World, which covers technology’s impact outside the West.

Silicon Valley’s artificial intelligence talent wars are now playing out in Asia.

OpenAI and Anthropic are poaching top talent from US tech giants including Google, Microsoft, and Amazon to build teams in countries like India and Singapore to sell their products and strengthen engagement with policymakers.

Last month, Meta’s India and Southeast Asia vice president, Sandhya Devanathan, left the company after a decade to join OpenAI as vice president for Southeast Asia and Australia. This was at least the ninth hire by a US AI giant from an American big tech firm in Asia in the past year.

“The number of executives in India who’ve actually run a country-level P&L [profit and loss] for a global tech company, negotiated with Indian regulators, and built enterprise trust at scale is small, maybe a few hundred people across all of Big Tech India,” Arjun Jaggi, an applied AI researcher and executive adviser to Fortune 500 companies, told Rest of World.

item.title: Russia: ‘Plague’ death is causing panic but there is little reason to worry for now
item.description: The availability of treatment, rapid testing and contact tracing mean the outlook of plague is very different today.
item.content:encoded:
A laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, Russia, has died just days after falling ill with an undisclosed illness.

While reports of suspected plague have been circulating in the media, Russia’s consumer health watchdog has described the illness as pneumonia of unknown cause. The World Health Organization also stated the official cause of death has not yet been confirmed. Plague therefore remains only a possible explanation.

While this is a tragic death and an important investigation, it’s certainly not a reason to panic or sign that the Black Death has returned. The availability of treatment, rapid testing and contact tracing mean the outlook of plague is very different today.

Why is plague suspected?

It’s currently not clear what the laboratory technician’s cause of death was. But as the research institute where she worked studies plague bacteria, health authorities are right to consider plague as a potential cause of illness.

The illness that she experienced – a form of pneumonia that ended in her death just a few days of contracting it – also resembles symptoms of pneumonic plague.

On Thursday night, Meta took down a viral video that purported to show Bharatiya Janata Party candidate Shankharav Sarkar going behind the screen of a polling booth where an electronic voting machine was placed during the bye-election for West Bengal’s Rejinagar Assembly constituency on October 6.

The video, posted by Golam Nabi Azad, the BJP’s principal opponent in the seat, was removed in compliance with a legal request from Indian authorities, according to a message that Meta overlaid on the post. The Aam Janata Unnayan Party leader in his Facebook post had described the bye-poll as an “unprecedented farce in the name of democracy”.

He alleged, “The BJP candidate himself has looted votes!”

On Tuesday, Scroll reporters in Rejinagar witnessed the police turning away Muslim voters from some polling stations. Opposition workers alleged that they were intimidated in the lead-up to the vote and some independent journalists said that the social media pages through which they disseminated their videos had also been blocked.

item.title: True Story: Why Gyanesh Kumar’s exit may not end the rigging of Indian elections
item.description: India’s election body has failed to check vote suppression in recent years.
item.content:encoded:
Delhi is under lockdown as the police have imposed unprecedented restrictions in the national capital to prevent young people from gathering at Jantar Mantar on October 10 to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The protests have been sparked by a recent report in the Indian Express that revealed that Kumar had kept his fellow election commissioners in the dark about crucial decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The exercise has disenfranchised millions of Indians.

But one resignation might not be enough to restore free and fair elections in the country since the problems with India’s election machinery run deep.

item.title: JNU sacks professor, a Congress MP, over sexual harassment allegations by students
item.description: Angomcha Bimol Akoijam had denied the allegations, stating that they had been made to tarnish his reputation.
item.content:encoded:
Jawaharlal Nehru University on Friday dismissed professor Angomcha Bimol Akoijam who had been accused of sexual harassment by 11 students, ANI reported.

Akoijam is a Congress Lok Sabha MP from Manipur.

The complaints of sexual harassment against Akoijam had been submitted to the university’s internal committee four months ago, The Times of India reported.

Akoijam, who lives on campus, has been accused of inviting students to his residence for gatherings and making sexual advances, the newspaper reported. Some complainants also alleged that he made allegedly lewd and inappropriate comments during classes and viva examinations, including demands for sexual acts in exchange for marks.

Akoijam had denied the allegations, accusing what he described as “racist schemers” attempting to tarnish his reputation with unverified claims and lies, India Today reported.

The university said on Friday that the allegations against Akoijam had been investigated by the internal committee. Based on the panel’s findings, the professor at the Centre for the Study of Social Systems was dismissed from service with immediate effect.

Responding to the development, Akoijam said he does not have the dismissal order, reported PTI.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Heat Chamber’ in ‘Anita Agnihotri: Selected Stories’, translated from the Bengali.

“Poobi! E…i Poobi!” Sheetli called her from the back, giggling.

Poobi ran off, remnants of food still on her fingers.

She was dressed in a floppy, faded gown, the one she was eating in. Hardly an elaborate meal – merely two ladles of rice scraped off the bottom of the pot. Poobi was waiting with a few stray shrimps and a sea of curry on her plate, confident that her mother would give her all the rice. She was chewing the shrimp shells with great concentration. But Poobi’s mother Chinta gave Sheetli the entire portion of rice without a second thought; Sheetli’s plate was dry, without any curry on it. And didn’t their mother know how big Poobi’s appetite was? She was absolutely famished this morning. A Delhi court on Friday granted former Wrestling Federation of India Chief Brij Bhushan Singh time to file his response to an appeal filed by four women wrestlers challenging his acquittal in a sexual harassment case, Live Law reported.

When the court asked the Delhi Police if it would challenge Singh’s acquittal, the public prosecutor said the decision was yet to be made and sought 15 days, reported PTI.

The court posted the matter for hearing next on October 28.

On August 3, Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Ashwini Panwar of Rouse Avenue Courts acquitted the former Bharatiya Janata Party MP and his co-accused Vinod Tomar, a former assistant secretary of the wrestling federation.

In his order, Panwar stated that the allegations against Singh were “false and fabricated” and seemed to be “politically motivated”.

item.title: ‘Does not advance shared ambitions’: MEA on US suspending IT firms from green card programme
item.description: New Delhi said that United States Vice President JD Vance’s remarks, describing foreign workers as ‘indentured servants’, was ‘unwarranted’.
item.content:encoded:
India on Friday said that the United States’ decision to suspend several information technology companies from the permanent labour certification programme goes against advancing the shared ambitions of the two countries.

Permanent labour certification is a process that employers must complete before filing petitions for most employment-based green cards. Under the programme, employers must establish that there are no qualified, willing and available US workers for a particular job.

Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft, Adobe and India-based information technology companies Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL are expected to be affected by the Donald Trump administration’s decision.

The Indian external affairs ministry said that the permanent labour certification programme is different from the H-1B visa programme, which allows companies in the US to temporarily employ foreign workers for special occupations.

The suspension of permanent labour certification applications does not affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the persons who hold the visa and their dependents, it said.

However, it said that there could be “some impact” on the Green Card process of eligible employees of the affected companies. A green card allows a foreign citizen to live and work permanently in the US.

item.title: Assam woman found dead near railway tracks after complaining of drunk men aboard train
item.description: While the railway police said they suspect she fell off the running train, her family alleged that she was murdered.
item.content:encoded:
A 20-year-old woman from Assam who had called her family to say that she was feeling unsafe aboard a train from Visakhapatnam to Guwahati was found dead beside a railway track in Srikakulam district of Andhra Pradesh on Wednesday, reported The Hindu.

While the railway police said they suspect Himashree Boro fell off the running train, her family alleged that she was murdered.

Boro, a college student from Guwahati, had travelled to Visakhapatnam for a dance competition. She boarded the Kanyakumari-Dibrugarh Vivek Express alone at around 12.15 am on Tuesday, reported The Times of India.

Soon after, she told a friend and family members that she was feeling uncomfortable in a coach full of “unruly, inebriated” men, reported The Indian Express.

She had reportedly also shared a video with her family from inside the train before her phone became unreachable around 3 am.

The family contacted the railway helpline and were told that Railway Protection Force personnel would check on Boro.

The police have registered a case under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita section relating to suspicious death.

item.title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay for promoting international law
item.description: Pillay, who is of Indian-Tamil origin, showed that legal measures can help prevent war and violence, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Peace Prize was on Friday awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Pillay, 85, was born into an Indian-origin Tamil family under apartheid in Durban. She has been “confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion”, said the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

Her commitment to universal legal principles and her “firm moral compass” are constants in a long career, the committee said. “A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time,” it added.

Pillay has “significantly enlarged the scope and impact” of international law, the panel said.

She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court.

Pillay was also the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. She is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide.

item.title: Bengal bye-polls: BJP wins Nandigram, Rejinagar
item.description: Polling was held on Tuesday, with the Opposition alleging that voters had been intimidated.
item.content:encoded:
The Bharatiya Janata Party won the Nandigram and Rejinagar Assembly bye-elections in West Bengal on Friday.

In Nandigram, BJP candidate Hasi Rani Rath defeated Congress candidate Milan Pradhan by more than 1.2 lakh votes.

Rath is mother of an aide to Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari who was shot dead two days after the state election results were announced in May.

The Trinamool Congress faction led by former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee decided to support Pradhan after the faction’s candidate had withdrawn her nomination, shortly after photographs of her meeting Adhikari were shared online.

The bye-poll became necessary after Adhikari vacated the seat. The chief minister had won the Nandigram and Bhabanipur seats during the state polls.

Adhikari has held the seat since 2016. He left the TMC and joined the BJP in December 2020, months ahead of the 2021 polls.

In Rejinagar, BJP’s Shankharavh Sarkar defeated Aam Janata Unnayan Party’s Golam Nabi Azad by more than 75,800 votes. Congress’ Abdullahil Kafi finished third and the Mamata Banerjee-led TMC group’s Rabiul Alam Chowdhury fourth.

The bye-election in the Muslim-majority constituency became necessary after Aam Janata Unnayan Party chief Humayun Kabir, who had won Rejinagar and Nowda in the May, decided to retain Nowda.

The Supreme Court on Friday barred the authorities in Delhi from imposing a complete closure of metro services in the national capital on Saturday during a protest at Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Bar and Bench reported.

A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant said that metro and other railway services must function “in a suitably regulated manner so that inconvenience to the public at large is minimised”.

The court also directed the authorities to publicise its decision about the curbs to avoid inconvenience to commuters.

item.title: Noida airport to be named after Narendra Modi
item.description: ‘Those who do not believe anybody would remember them want to name structures after themselves in their lifetime,’ said Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav.
item.content:encoded:
The international airport in Noida will be named after Prime Minister Narendra Modi, announced Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Adityanath on Friday.

The airport, located in Jewar on the outskirts of the city, is currently named Noida International Airport. Flights began in June.

The proposal to change the name was passed by the state Cabinet, the chief minister said.

Reacting to this, Samajwadi Party President Akhilesh Yadav said that facilities and institutions are usually named after eminent persons to remember them.

“Those who do not believe anybody would remember them want to name structures after themselves in their lifetime,” said Yadav. “We have no objection to it. But, the chief minister who has changed the name of the airport, residents of Uttar Pradesh are about to vote him out.”

April 16, 1971

Dhiman was sitting beside Ma on the bed, munching on peanuts and picturing a monkey floating down a river on a log. The current mathematical problem he was wrestling with involved calculating the speed of the river’s current if the monkey covered a distance of 250 kilometres in 200 minutes, and the speed of the monkey was 60 kilometres per hour.

The sweet floral scent that filled the small room was calming in the middle of his monkey problems. It came from the jasmine oil Ma used for her hair, as she had done for as long as he could remember.

“Priti! Priti!” His father, Bijoy Lahiri, burst into the small room in their rented two-bedroom flat at Entally, central Calcutta, as Ma leaned over to look at the numbers Dhiman had scrawled in his homework notebook. “Can you serve me dinner, please?”

item.title: ‘Reporting Live’ review: A solid thriller about crusading journalism
item.description: Dhruv Tripathi’s Hindi-language film is out on Netflix.
item.content:encoded:
Television reporter Sandhya and cameraman Vinod might quarrel like siblings, but they are a well-matched team, chasing stories of land grabbing and corruption in high places for their network Azaad Bharati. A bridge collapse in a village near Mumbai lead Sandhya (Parineeti Chopra) and Vinod (Deven Bhojani) to their biggest ever investigation.

A sand mafia is hard at work, dredging up “brown gold” over the permitted limit and ruining the local ecology. Sandhya and Vinod meet whistle blowers Shiva (Amol Palekar) and Mangesh (Pitobash Tripathy), who give them vital tip-offs but also warn of them of the dangers that lie ahead. Back at the head office, their boss Vidur (Adil Hussain) gets into spats with the channel owner Shyam (Shekhar Suman) about editorial freedom.

Dhruv Tripathi’s Hindi film is out on Netflix. Although the screenplay by Tripathi and Mihir Jadhav doesn’t break new ground, the 115-minute movie is tightly plotted and efficiently narrated. Staged in the mould of American conspiracy thrillers, in which the rot goes all the way to the top, the thriller gives a reasonable sense of the challenges faced by fearless dissenters.

The Allahabad High Court on Thursday questioned the use of the term “andolanjeevi” in the grounds for detaining journalist Satyam Verma under the National Security Act after the workers’ protests in Noida, Live Law reported.

“Where did this term ‘andolanjeevi’ come from?” the court was quoted as asking verbally. “How did it find its way into an official document?”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi first used the term in 2021 during protests against the now-repealed farm laws, describing protesters as a new category of people who “are like parasites who feed off protests”.

The bench of Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev was hearing Verma’s petition challenging his detention under the National Security Act. The Act allows for long periods of detention without trial up to a year.

During the hearing, the bench perused the detention order dated May 12, issued by Gautam Buddh Nagar District Magistrate Medha Roopam, and the grounds of detention supplied to Verma.

item.title: ‘Eyes’ review: A clear-eyed look at a culture of stalking and abuse
item.description: The seven-episode Malayalam series is out on Sony LIV.
item.content:encoded:
The title of the Malayalam show Eyes refers to a programme that monitors men who harass, maim or kill the women they claim to love. The Sony LIV series is also about seeing gender violence for what it is, and what it does to people.

The task force “Eyes” is set up after an increase in brazen attacks by stalkers. Reasoning that conventional forms of punishment are ineffective, the focus shifts towards treating offenders, while also tracking them through a software developed by criminal psychologist Vidya (Shruthi Ramachandran).

The idea, at least on paper, is to catch men before they can brutalise women, while also understanding the attackers better. But the gap between textbook lessons and actual behaviour is often vast.

item.title: Infosys, Tata, Wipro among Indian IT firms suspended from US green card programme

The United States on Thursday suspended information technology companies Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe from the Permanent Labor Certification Programme. The process allows employers to sponsor foreign workers, including H-1B visa holders, for employment-based green cards.

Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL are India-based IT firms.

The action does not cancel existing H-1B visas held by employees of these companies. Permanent Labor Certification is a separate process that employers must complete before filing petitions for most employment-based green cards. Under the programme, employers must establish that there are no qualified, willing and available US workers for a particular job.

A green card allows a foreign citizen to live and work permanently in the US. H-1B visas allow companies in the US to temporarily employ foreign workers for special occupations.

The move is part of a broader immigration crackdown under President Donald Trump, whose second term began in January 2025.

On Thursday, US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said that the Department of Labor would “not accept any new or process any pending Permanent Labor Certification applications” involving the companies.

The Andhra Pradesh government has declared a drought in 21 of its 28 districts as the rainfall deficit from June to August in the state stood at 53%, reported The Hindu on Thursday.

The deficit in rainfall was due to the effects of El Niño, which is a phenomenon that involves the warming of ocean surface temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific. It typically occurs every few years and has been linked to reduced monsoon rainfall in India.

“An average rainfall of 197.6 mm has been received against the normal rainfall of 424.3 mm from June 1 to August 31,” The Indian Express quoted the government order as saying.

The government declared the drought for the Kharif season on October 1, reported The Hindu. Such declarations are typically made at the end of October.

The Kharif season in India is between June and October.

item.title: Is 2026 the beginning of the end of the Modi era?
item.description: When protests begin attracting large numbers of people who are willing to risk police beatings, it is usually a sign of anti-incumbency setting in.

In 2011, Delhi became the epicentre of protests that three years later, culminated in the toppling of the Manmohan Singh government.

Fifteen years later, the national capital is once again aflame with protests. Will they similarly build up momentum for political change in 2029?

There are strong parallels between 2011 and 2026.

In 2011, after protests in Jantar Mantar in April, Ramlila Maidan saw two rounds of mass demonstrations – the first in June, the second in August.

This year, barely two months after young people took over Jantar Mantar in June, a second wave is building up, with the police this week blocking even Opposition leaders from reaching the protest square.

In 2011, it was about “corruption”. In 2026, it is about “rigging” – of exam papers, of the election system. The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature was on Thursday awarded to Canadian poet, essayist, translator, classicist, and professor Anne Carson “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”. She is 76, and is the second writer from Canada to win the award (after Alice Munro in 2013).

The prestigious award, bestowed by 18 judges who make up the Swedish Academy, honours a writer’s entire body of work and is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or about $1.2 million (about Rs 11.6 crore).

The Nobel Prize website said: “Anne Carson has, throughout her entire career, combined poetry writing with translation work and teaching at various universities. Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning. She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work.”

Carson’s oeuvre across forms and genres comprises more than 30 works. Among her notable works are Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse (1998), Norma Jean Baker of Troy: a version of Euripides’ Helen (2019) and translations of Sophocles’s Electra, and of Euripides’s Grief Lessons: Four Plays.

item.title: Punjab’s prisons are awash with de-addiction pills. But is that good news?

In 2017, the Punjab government introduced a new therapy for victims of drug abuse.

It involved putting users of opioids like heroin – colloquially called chitta – on a combination of less potent opioids to wean them off their addiction.

The substitute – buprenorphine and naloxone pills – was meant to be taken orally and under medical supervision. According to a psychiatrist who works in one of Punjab’s central jails, the therapy drastically reduced the vulnerability of an addict.

“Firstly, there is no intravenous use because of which an addict is likely to get infected with HIV, hepatitis or other diseases,” he said. “There is almost zero chance of drug overdose death.”

The therapy was rolled out across more than 529 clinics over the years and met with limited success. In November 2023, the Punjab government informed the Assembly that around 80-90% of patients who complete this treatment at the state’s Outpatient Opioid Assisted Treatment clinics relapse into addiction.

item.title: Maritime history: How merchants transcended caste and faith identity to rule over sea trade
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Indians in the Ocean: Cultures of Trade and Travel ca 1000-1500 CE’, by Mahmood Kooria.
item.content:encoded:
Major maritime merchant communities from the subcontinent transcended religious, regional and caste identities. In the existing literature, they are often identified along these lines, yet such classifications do not fully capture the fluid and interconnected nature of their networks, as in the case of Banias, which included Buddhists and Jains earlier, but also Hindus and even Muslims later. The same goes with Lohanas as well as Klings and Chulias, all who crossed the borders of religions as much as of the regions. It would be impossible to enlist and analyse all mercantile groups from the subcontinent here, but below I provide snapshots of a few major transoceanic communities active between the 11th and 16th centuries.

Until the end of the first millennium in the subcontinent, Buddhist and Jain traders played a major role in the oceanic world, often mirroring their influence in overland commerce. The boundaries between these groups in the maritime mercantile contexts were blurry, but we do see occasional references for them competing for economic and political influence.

Over the past decade, India has seen climate change take a deadly toll in the form of extreme weather and disasters such as landslides and glacial collapse.

How did these concerns resonate in the Indian Parliament?

In the last 10 years, Parliament maintained a steady focus on climate change, but its attention has centered largely on setting ambitious goals and announcing national targets.

Much of the strip lies in ruins and more than 74,000 Palestinians are dead, with thousands more believed to remain buried under the rubble.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded on Wednesday to two chemists for their research into the mirror images of molecules, which is decisive for the development of pharmaceuticals.

Henri Kagan, 95, is a professor at the Université Paris-Sud in France. He is a French citizen. Kenso Soai, a 76-year-old Japanese citizen, is a professor at the Tokyo University of Science.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said that they were being honoured for the discovery of “non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.

Some molecules, such as amino acids, exist as two variants that are each other’s mirror image. However, living organisms only contain one of these mirror images.

“How chemical asymmetry such as this could have emerged was long a mystery to chemists,” the academy said, adding that Kagan and Soai discovered “a solution to this puzzle”.

Their discoveries have been “decisive for chemists who design reactions” for manufacturing pharmaceuticals, it added.

The two chemists will equally share the prize amount of 12 million Swedish kronor, or Rs 11.5 crore.

The Reserve Bank of India on Wednesday increased the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5%.

The repo rate is the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks. The Monetary Policy Committee reviews the rate every two months.

This was the first hike in the lending rate in nearly four years. The last hike was in February 2023, when the Reserve Bank of India raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 6.5%.

Central banks usually increase key lending rates to control inflation. Higher key lending rates translate to higher interest on loans disbursed by commercial banks. This, in turn, keeps a check on discretionary spending by consumers which is expected to help curb price rise due to high inflation.

The committee had cut the repo rate by 25 basis points from 5.5% to 5.25% in December and kept it unchanged in February, April, June and August.

A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Basis points are used to describe changes in interest rates and other financial instruments.

The committee also changed its monetary policy stance to “calibrated tightening” from “neutral”. The shift signals that the central bank is now more focused on containing inflation.

item.title: How Netanyahu and Modi turn security failures into political weapons
item.description: Their strategy is to make citizens more afraid of the enemy than angry with the government that failed them.
item.content:encoded:
The passengers aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv survived because a wounded captain, some passengers and reserve pilots prevented a disaster.

When they returned to Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was there to welcome them. It was a perfect opportunity for photographs: Netanyahu standing beside passengers of a plane who had escaped death. Missing from the public discussion was the question his government needed to answer. Why had their survival depended on a heavily injured pilot doing what a robust security system should have made unnecessary?

The September 30 flight had come close to disaster when its Omani copilot, Hamam al-Hammami, allegedly attacked the Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, with a crash axe. Despite his injuries, Machchhar opened the cockpit door, reportedly allowing passengers to overpower the attacker. The aircraft eventually safely landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

But this cannot serve as an excuse for the failures that endangered the passengers.

Those failures extend beyond the cockpit. The United Arab Emirates, from where the flight started, says that Israel received the passenger and crew details before departure. I remember how Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and other Commonwealth leaders failed to persuade Britain’s Margaret Thatcher at a 1986 summit in London to stiffen sanctions against apartheid. Thatcher’s reaction was rigid because the Soviet paranoia still plagued the West. That is why she advanced a lame excuse for not weakening the White apartheid regime.

“More sanctions would hurt Black workers,” she argued.

item.title: Ethiopia is slipping into a war again that could expand to more countries
item.description: The conflicts will intersect with the civil war in neighboring Sudan, causing a complicated, regionwide conflagration.
item.content:encoded:
Four years after a fragile ceasefire ended widespread conflict in Ethiopia, the region is again slipping back into full-out war.

On September 23, 2026, advancing soldiers of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front seized government positions in northern Ethiopia.

It followed the announcement of a new alliance of seven armed movements in opposition to the Ethiopian government and deteriorating relations between the country and neighboring Eritrea, which it accuses of supporting the new alliance.

As an expert on conflict in the Horn of Africa and Ethiopian national security, I know the spiraling conditions now have been long in the making.

The November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement ended immediate fighting between Ethiopia and Tigrayan rebels, but it did not constitute a comprehensive peace settlement. Crucially, it was never followed by wider political negotiations to address the root causes of the war. The concern now is that the conflicts will intersect with the civil war in neighboring Sudan, causing a complicated, regionwide conflagration.

How has the conflict escalated?

The September 23 ground offensive by the TPLF drew global attention to the situation in Ethiopia. But in reality, the ratcheting up of tensions between the federal government in Addis Ababa and the TPLF has been going on for months.

Eleven Indians were injured in an attack on a commercial ship while passing through the Strait of Hormuz, off the coast of Oman, on Tuesday, the Ministry of External Affairs said.

The projectile hit the Panama-flagged MT On Peace, which had 19 crew members on board, including 17 Indians. Twelve people were injured in the attack.

Eleven Indian seafarers have been killed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in West Asia began, in attacks involving four Indian ships and 60 foreign-flagged vessels.

The ministry condemned Tuesday’s attack and said that such incidents remained a cause of “deep concern” for India.

“We reiterate our call for an immediate cessation of such attacks in the interests of peace and stability in the region,” it said.

item.title: Bangladesh measles outbreak claims 900 lives – and serves as warning for why vaccination matters
item.description: Even a small dip in vaccination rates can leave pockets of unprotected children.
item.content:encoded:
Almost 900 people in Bangladesh are suspected to have died in a measles outbreak that began in March. Most of those affected are children.

Measles is one of the most infectious diseases known. It can spread rapidly when vaccination rates fall, and the Bangladesh outbreak shows how quickly years of gaps in protection can turn into a serious public health crisis.

The country had hoped to eliminate measles and rubella by 2020. Instead, the pandemic disrupted routine childhood vaccinations, leaving pockets of children vulnerable to the virus. Now other countries where vaccination rates have fallen face a similar risk.

Vaccine hesitancy is probably part of the story here too. During the Covid pandemic, almost half of Bangladesh’s population were wary of getting vaccinated. That same wariness may well have carried over to the measles-rubella jab, with many parents simply refusing to let their children be vaccinated.

Measles has its own set of drivers, too. Poverty, education levels, and how often mothers attend antenatal check-ups all shape whether children in a community end up vaccinated. Add it all up, and childhood vaccination coverage has been sliding for years – down to just 87%.

item.title: Francis Halzen awarded physics Nobel for discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin
item.description: His ‘vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental’ for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, said the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Prize in Physics was on Tuesday awarded to Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin and his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.

Halzen, 82, is a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the United States.

“His vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors,” the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.

The observatory is near the South Pole in Antarctica. Using the observatory, researchers “can capture neutrinos from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe”, the academy added.

Halzen first presented his vision for capturing neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988. When a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus, it produces a flash of light that can be tracked by sensors in the glacial ice.

He will receive a prize amount of 12 million Swedish krona, or Rs 11.5 crore.

On Monday, the Nobel Prize in medicine was jointly awarded to three scientists – Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth – for their research on brain activity.

The Nobel Prize in chemistry will be announced on Wednesday, literature on Thursday and for peace on Friday. The prize in economics will be announced on October 12.

item.description: Mohan Yadav said that the cash transfer programme for women announced by BJP ahead of Assembly polls had turned out to be ‘a very costly affair’.
item.content:encoded:
Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav has said that he had not anticipated the “financial burden” that his government’s cash transfer scheme for women, the Ladli Behna Yojana, would cause the state, reported NDTV on Monday.

“The Ladli Behna scheme turned out to be a very costly affair,” the Bharatiya Janata Party leader said at an event in Bhopal.

His party had announced the scheme six months ahead of the Assembly elections in 2023. Launched by former Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan, the scheme entailed monthly transfer of Rs 1,000 to women between 21 and 60 years of age, whose annual family income does not exceed Rs 2.5 lakh.

The Maharashtra government on Monday announced a minimum 10% water cut in all urban areas from October 16, citing a “significant decrease in rainfall” caused by the El Niño weather phenomenon.

The El Niño weather phenomenon involves the warming of ocean surface temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific. It typically occurs every few years and has been linked to reduced monsoon rainfall in India.

In September, the Maharashtra government had declared drought conditions in 74% of the state’s subdistricts amid a deficit in rainfall during the southwest monsoon season.

On Monday, state Minister of Water Resources Girish Mahajan said that the department has issued directives to use water with “extreme frugality and implement stringent measures”. He added that top priority has been given to ensure preventing any shortage of drinking water.

The new water strategy will be in force until August 31, said Mahajan, adding that effects of the El Niño are likely to last into the coming year.

The state government’s plan also outlines the need to curb water leakage and ensure that sewage treatment plants are operated at full capacity.

Water for irrigation will be allocated only after meeting the requirements for drinking water, livestock and fodder, according to the plan.

item.title: The world order is ‘complicated’. Can Indian foreign policy navigate ‘situationships’?
item.description: New Delhi’s global posturing has always coexisted with a pragmatic practice closer to home.
item.content:encoded:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s much-discussed special address at Davos in January called for a world of “values-based realism.” First proposed by Finland’s President, Alexander Stubb, values-based realism describes not a strategy, but an “instrument – temporary, adaptive, and situational…that espouses values while engaging respectfully with those who do not share them.”

Put more colloquially, this macro-geopolitical landscape operates exactly like a Gen Z “situationship” – relationships that are not beholden to labels, exclusivity, and can be non-committal.

India, with its cautious diplomatic language and history of moral rhetoric on the global stage, may not seem like a player suited to this new world of “situationships.” Yet New Delhi’s record navigating problematic regimes in its own neighborhoods suggests that India may actually enter this new order with more experience than most.

Situationships and values-based realism

Where once the rules-based international order was the organising principle for global affairs, the broader strategic framework increasingly gaining traction is values-based realism, which underscores the rising salience of variable, issue-by-issue geometries that form when states choose immediate interests over long-term normative alignment.

item.title: Missives from the heart: When Hindi cinema put the letter to song
item.description: From flowers tucked into envelopes and lovers who needed postmen to write for them, Hindi films knew that a letter could carry much more than a message.
item.content:encoded:
Historians spend a surprising amount of time reading other people’s letters. Love letters, family letters, petitions, complaints, advice, requests for money, quarrels between husbands and wives, messages written from prison or pardes. Having spent years among Hindi archives full of such correspondence, I began to notice another archive of letters that had been sitting in plain sight all along. Hindi cinema is full of them.

There are khat, chitthi, patra, paati, sandesa and paigham. There are envelopes and postcards, postmen and pigeons, letters dictated to someone else, letters carrying flowers, letters from home and letters that never arrive. Some are read. Some are sung. Some seem capable of containing an entire person.

item.title: A new book examines why rural women are undergoing sterilisation despite ambivalence about surgery
item.description: An excerpt from ‘State Intimacies: Sterilization, Care and Reproductive Chronicity in Rural North India’, by Eva Fiks.
item.content:encoded:
While wider biomedical discourses focus on the laparoscope’s convenience, rural women often resist this simplistic understanding and draw on their everyday lives to develop an understanding of how this technology works. The way that the laparoscope enters everyday conversations of rural Rajasthani women – what it is, how it works and whether it is better than open surgery – uncovers women’s relationships with population control efforts, the fascination with technology, and power exercised by the state and biomedical institutions. The relationship between women and laparoscopes encapsulates the reasons why tubal ligation is seen by some people as a technologically sophisticated option that is implemented by “choice”, in contrast to the widespread concerns about the quality of care and numerous women’s deaths in sterilisation camps in a population control programme often described as a form of violence against women.

Across India, tubal ligation is often referred to as an operation. Women in my field site often specify what type of operation they have had: open surgery or a laparoscopic tubectomy. They refer to open surgery as bara (big) operation, tankewala (with stitches) operation or hathwala (done by hand) operation. item.title: How El Niño is causing droughts in parts of the world and floods elsewhere
item.description: It is a result of climactic conditions being shaped by the warming Pacific Ocean and the air above it.
item.content:encoded:
The Pacific Ocean is warming unusually quickly, and this year’s El Niño has already surpassed previous records. Forecasters expect it to strengthen even further before approaching its usual peak around December.

El Niño, the warm phase of a natural fluctuation in the Earth’s climate system, can reshape weather thousands of miles away, bringing drought to some regions while increasing the risk of heavy rain and flooding in others. To understand why, you need to follow what happens to the Pacific’s warm water – and the air above it.

Usually, winds over the tropical Pacific blow from east to west, pushing warm surface water towards the western Pacific, where it piles up around Indonesia and nearby regions. These are the trade winds. As warm water moves westward, colder water from deeper in the ocean rises to replace it in the east – a process called upwelling. This is why the western Pacific is usually much warmer than the eastern Pacific.

item.title: Scabies: The invisible skin infection that is more than skin-deep
item.description: A series on health conditions that disproportionately affects marginalised communities.
item.content:encoded:
What is it like to itch all the time, to lose sleep every night, to be dazed in the classroom and accept this as normal?

For many months now, 12-year-old Budhram’s* skin had been itching incessantly. Three of the ten boys in his dormitory at a residential school for Baiga Adivasis (a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group) in Chattisgarh had the same problem. Back home, Budhram’s younger siblings and mother also had an itch that refused to go away.

This story of daily, mass torment is common across India – from Kondh tribals in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh to the labouring poor of Bihar and Gujarat. Entire villages may have a disease that has afflicted humanity for millenia, but remains neglected by patients and public health authorities alike – scabies.

For Budhram, living with scabies means unrelenting, uncontrollable itching that keeps him awake at night and hampers his concentration at school during the day. Some local practitioners’ injections provide only partial relief, at a high recurring cost. Meanwhile, years of sleepless nights compounded by hunger, anemia and hard physical labour have robbed his mother of a good life. She has collapsed from exhaustion on more than one occasion.

The film’s title refers both to the local name of the Great Indian Bustard and the whiskey brand from Diageo India, which supports the conservation programme and has backed the film’s production.
